summary: Proposes two changes to the ARPANET host access protocol: logical addressing, so host addresses do not depend on physical location, and a shorter time that a host can be blocked by its IMP. Replaced by RFC 851.

plainLanguage.summary: Two ideas for how computers plug into the old ARPANET: addresses that follow a machine around, and not making it wait as long when the network is busy.

questions: how does arpanet host blocking work
what is the name declaration message
subtitle: Logical addressing and improved host blocking for the ARPANET 1822 protocol.

tldr.problem: The original ARPANET 1822 protocol used physical addresses based on host location in the network, and hosts could be blocked from sending messages for up to 15 seconds when the IMP was busy, creating inefficiency.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 802 introduces two changes: (1) logical addressing (1822L names and addresses) that are independent of physical location, allowing host mobility and load sharing, and (2) a short-blocking feature that limits blocking to 100 milliseconds to 2 seconds, letting the host send other messages while waiting.
tldr.outcome: The 1822L protocol allows hosts to move without changing their network identity and improves responsiveness during network congestion by limiting blocking time. The RFC was replaced by RFC 851.

today: RFC 802 is a historical document describing an early ARPANET protocol proposal from 1981. It was replaced by RFC 851, which contains the actual as-implemented specification. The document is significant in the history of network protocols, demonstrating early solutions to host addressing and flow control problems that remain relevant today.

sections.title: Motivation for Changes
sections.content:
The original ARPANET 1822 protocol served the network well but had practical limitations. In the 1822 protocol, host addresses were tied to a specific location on the network—a host could not move from one port to another without using a different address. Additionally, when an ARPANET IMP (Interface Message Processor—a networking device) needed time to process a message, it would block all further input from that host for up to 15 seconds. This blocking strategy prevented other messages—which might be processed quickly—from being transmitted.

RFC 802 proposes two major enhancements to address these limitations. First, logical addressing allows a host to be known by a network-wide name independent of its physical location. Second, a short-blocking feature limits blocking duration to 100 milliseconds to 2 seconds, allowing hosts to send other messages while the IMP gathers resources. Both improvements retain full backward compatibility with the existing 1822 protocol.
sections.plainLanguage: Imagine a post office that won't take your mail if the person you're sending to is busy, and you have to wait 15 seconds. These changes let computers move without changing their address, and the post office will take other mail while getting ready for the big one.

sections.title: Logical Addressing: Names and Addresses
sections.content:
The 1822L protocol introduces two new forms of host identification alongside the original 1822 address. 1822L names are 16-bit logical identifiers assigned by a network administrator. Unlike 1822 addresses, these names are location-independent: a host keeps the same 1822L name even if it moves to a different physical port. Multiple hosts can share the same name (for load sharing), and one host can use multiple names (for multi-homing).

1822L addresses form a subset of the 1822L name space and specify a particular physical host port at a particular IMP. They allow 1822L hosts to directly address a specific location when needed. A host on a C/30 IMP is assigned at least one 1822L name when it comes online; it declares which names it wants to use by sending a Name Declaration Message (NDM) to its IMP. The IMP validates the names against a central database, informs the host which names are now effective, and translates incoming messages accordingly.
sections.plainLanguage: Instead of saying 'the computer at port 3 on IMP 5', you can now say 'Alice's computer', and Alice's computer can move to a different port and keep the same name. The network's post office knows where Alice is and gets her mail to the right place.

sections.title: The Short-Blocking Feature
sections.content:
In the original 1822 protocol, when an IMP receives a message, it allocates internal resources (connection setup, buffer space at the destination, etc.) before accepting it. If these resources are not immediately available due to network congestion, the IMP blocks the entire host—refusing all further input until the resources are obtained, which can take 15 seconds or more.

The short-blocking feature replaces this strategy with a timeout-based approach. When a host submits a message flagged for short-blocking, the IMP will either accept it immediately or, if resources cannot be gathered within a short timeout (100 milliseconds to 2 seconds), reject it with a specific reason code and allow the host to send other messages. Common blocking reasons include connection setup delay, end-to-end flow control (the destination host is not ready to receive), destination IMP buffer shortage, and network congestion. The host can resubmit the rejected message later, hopefully when conditions have improved, while other messages from the same host can proceed in the meantime.
sections.plainLanguage: If the post office is busy, instead of telling your computer 'wait 15 seconds', it says 'I can't handle this big package right now, but you can send other mail' and your computer can keep going. You can try that big package again later.

sections.title: 1822L Leader Format and Message Types
sections.content:
The 1822L protocol uses new message headers (called leaders) that differ from the original 1822 format. The Host-to-IMP leader is a 96-bit header containing: the 1822L flag identifying it as an 1822L message, the handling type (priority, trace, flags), message type (regular, error, NOP, Name Declaration Message, etc.), source and destination 1822L names (16 bits each), message ID, and sub-type. Regular messages (type 0) can specify sub-types: standard (full IMP services), standard with short-blocking, uncontrolled with short-blocking, or fully uncontrolled.

The IMP-to-Host leader mirrors the format but uses an IMP-specific flag instead of the host flag. One important message type is the Name Declaration Message (NDM), which the host uses to declare which of its 1822L names it wants to use. The NDM contains a list of names and a 0 or 1 bit for each, indicating whether that name should be effective or non-effective. The IMP replies with which names are now active, performing validation against the central name database.
sections.plainLanguage: Each message has a header that says what kind of message it is, who it is from, who it is for, and special instructions like 'this is important' or 'it is okay to drop this if you are too busy'.

sections.title: Implementation and Status
sections.content:
RFC 802 is explicitly a proposal, not a description of an implemented system. The document notes that the described features are subject to change based on responses and constraints discovered during implementation, though significant changes were not expected. The short-blocking feature and 1822L protocol were designed to be implemented on C/30 IMPs only; hosts on older Honeywell and Pluribus IMPs could not use the full 1822L capabilities, though they could still communicate with 1822L hosts using 1822 addresses and protocols.

RFC 802 was replaced by RFC 851, which contains the actual as-implemented specification after development was complete. The RFC remains historically important as documentation of ARPANET protocol evolution and the early design solutions for host addressing and flow control that influenced later internet protocols.
sections.plainLanguage: This was an early design proposal that was actually built and tested, then a later document described exactly what was built. This old protocol showed designers how to solve problems that modern internet protocols still solve today.
